problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of decreasing $x$ where $x>0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,m,$ its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is $4(1+2x)\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has a displacement of $1\,m$ when its velocity is $-4\,m/s,$ find $v$ in terms of $x.$
worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14070816/assets/466c0aa389beb6d1a42092b73bae75508ef2c50f1f08cca5efaac20d25615f30.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $4(1+2x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=4(1+2x).
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=4(1+2x).
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int 4(1+2x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=4(x+{x}^{2})+C.
$$

Now, since $x=1\,\text{m}$ when $v=-4\,\text{m/s},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =4(x+{x}^{2})+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(-4)^{2} & =4(1+{1}^{2})+C \\ 8 & =8+C \\ C & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =4(x+{x}^{2})+0 \\ {v}^{2} & =8(x+{x}^{2}) \\ v & =\pm 2\sqrt{2(x+{x}^{2})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)<0,$ so we can discard the positive square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=-2\sqrt{2(x+{x}^{2})}.
$$
